strong_form: Mainstream media coverage collapses two independent axes (support vs. opposition to elite-favored policies, e.g. high immigration or trade liberalization; and moral decency vs. bigotry) into one, so that people who oppose such a policy on principled, non-bigoted grounds are disproportionately portrayed as bigots, compared with how equally principled supporters are portrayed.
weak_form: Some coverage conflates policy opposition with prejudice, making nuanced dissenting positions hard to communicate.
refuted_if: Content analysis showing that coverage of principled opponents of elite-favored policies attributes bigotry no more often than warranted by their stated reasoning, or no more often than coverage attributes bad motives to supporters; or audiences reliably distinguishing the axes in coverage.

strongest_criticism: As stated it is a model fitted to anecdotes (e.g. one interview) with no systematic content analysis; 'principled opponent' is defined by the claimant, so any bigotry charge can be dismissed as misclassification, making it hard to refute. The asymmetry is also untested: supporters of elite policy are routinely painted as corrupt or treasonous by other outlets, so the effect may be partisan-media-wide rather than elite-direction-specific.
